t: What is an Agent • In the context of Artificial Intelligence (Al), intelligent agents are systems that perceive their environment, make decisions based on that perception, and take actions to achieve specific goals. • They are fundamental components of Al systems, which aim to mimic human intelligence by solving problems in dynamic environments. • The agent operates autonomously, meaning it is not directly controlled by a human operator.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 3
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Components of an Al System PERCEPTION REASONING ENVIRONMENT AGENT An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on the environment through actuators. Human: sensors are eyes, ears, actuators (effectors) are hands, legs, mouth. Robot: sensors are cameras, sonar, lasers, ladar, bump and actuators are grippers, manipulators, motors ACTION The agent's behavior is described by its function that maps perception to action.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 4
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Characteristics of Agent • Perceiving its environment: Using sensors (such as cameras, microphones, or software APls for virtual agents) to gather information about its surroundings. • Taking actions: Using actuators or output mechanisms (such as motors in robots, or software commands in virtual agents) to affect its environment. • Goal-Oriented Behavior: An Al agent operates to achieve predefined goals or objectives based on the information it gathers from its environment.

subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Example of Agent • A self-driving car is an Al agent that perceives its environment (road conditions, traffic, pedestrians) using cameras and sensors. • It processes this information to make decisions (steering, accelerating, braking) and acts accordingly to reach its destination safely.

t: What is Environment • The environment is the external world or context within which the agent operates. • It provides input to the agent and reacts to the agent's actions. • In Al, environments can vary greatly in complexity and predictability.

t: • Fully Observable vs. Partially Observable Term Fully Observable Partially Observable Meaning The agent has complete information about the environment at any given time. It can "see" everything it needs to make decisions. The agent has limited or incomplete information about the environment. It must make guesses or use memory. Example Chess: The agent knows the full state of the board and both players' pieces. Self-driving car: Sensors cannot detect every detail (hidden pedestrians, fog). The view is partial.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 9
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: 2. Deterministic vs. Stochastic (or Strategic) Term Deterministic Meaning The next state of the environment is completely determined by the current state and the agent's action - no randomness. Stochastic / Strategic The next state is not completely predictable; randomness or other agents' actions affect the result. Example Solving a math problem: If you apply correct steps, you always get the same answer. Poker: Depends on chance (cards drawn) and other players' strategies.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 10
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Term Episodic Sequential 3. Episodic vs. Sequential Meaning Each action is independent of the previous ones — no memory or dependency. Current actions affect future decisions or states. The agent needs to plan ahead. Example Image recognition: Classifying each image doesn't depend on previous ones. Chess or driving: A move now affects all future possibilities.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 11
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Term Static Dynamic 4. Static vs. Dynamic Meaning The environment does not change while the agent is deciding what to do. The environment keeps changing - even as the agent decides or acts. Example Crossword puzzle: The puzzle doesn't change while you think. Traffic system: Vehicles move continuously; you must react in real time.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 12
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Term Discrete Continuous 5. Discrete vs. Continuous Meaning Environment has a finite number of distinct states, actions, or time steps. States and actions can vary smoothly - infinite possibilities. Example Chess: Fixed grid, limited moves. Self-driving car: Steering angle, speed, and road curvature vary continuously.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 13
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: 6. Single Agent vs. Multiagent Term Single Agent Meaning Only one agent operates in the environment. Example Autonomous vacuum cleaner: Works alone. Multiagent Mutiple agents interact or compete/cooperate within the same environment. Online chess game: Two intelligent agents (players) interact.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 34

t: Types of Agents • Simple Reflex Agents: - These agents make decisions based purely on the current situation and predefined rules. - They don't consider the history or future consequences of their actions. - Example: A thermostat that turns on the heater if the temperature drops below a certain point.

t: Types of Agents • Model-Based Reflex Agents: - These agents maintain an internal state or model of the world, allowing them to handle partial observability and make decisions based on both current inputs and their history. - Example: A robot vacuum cleaner that builds a map of a room as it cleans.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 39
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Types of Agents • Goal-Based Agents: - These agents make decisions by considering future consequences and whether an action will help achieve a specific goal. - Example: A chess-playing Al that evaluates possible future moves to checkmate the opponent.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 40

t: Types of Agents • Utility-Based Agents: - These agents go beyond simple goal achievement and try to maximize a utility function (a measure of success or satisfaction). - They seek not only to reach a goal but to achieve the best possible outcome. - Example: A self-driving car that not only reaches its destination but does so in the safest, quickest, and most comfortable way.

t: Nature of Environment and Agents • Nature of the Environment - Understanding the nature of the environment is crucial for designing an effective agent. - Based on the environment's properties (deterministic vs. stochastic, static vs. dynamic, etc.), the agent must adapt its strategies. • In a deterministic, fully observable environment, an agent can plan its actions ahead with certainty (like playing chess). • In a dynamic, stochastic, and partially observable environment, an agent may need to rely on probabilistic models and adaptive strategies (like a drone navigating through unpredictable weather conditions).

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 50
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Nature of Environment and Agents • Nature of the Agent - The design of an agent depends on the complexity of the problem it's solving and the nature of the environment it interacts with. - The agent's architecture includes: • Sensors to perceive the environment. • Effectors or actuators to act on the environment. • Decision-making algorithms (such as search algorithms, learning algorithms, or rule-based systems) to choose appropriate actions.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 51
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Problem Solving Agent • A problem-solving agent is a type of intelligent agent designed to find solutions to specific problems by exploring the search space, which contains all possible states or configurations. • These agents aim to find a sequence of actions that leads to the desired goal state from a given initial state.

label: Agent & Environment deck, slide 52
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Steps in Problem Solving by an Agent • Formulate the Problem: - The agent defines the initial state, the possible actions, and the goal state. - Example: In a maze-solving robot, the problem is to find the shortest path from the entrance to the exit. • Search for a Solution: - The agent explores the search space, trying different sequences of actions to find the one that reaches the goal. - Example: The robot might use algorithms like depth-first search (DFS) or A* to explore all possible paths in the maze. • Execute the Solution: - Once a solution is found, the agent executes the actions to achieve the goal. - Example: The robot follows the path to exit the maze.

t: Characteristics of Al Problem Al problems are generally complex and require intelligent behavior to reach a solution. The characteristics of an Al problem describe the fundamental aspects that make a problem suitable for solving using Al techniques. Here are the key characteristics: • Non-Deterministic: Al problems often have outcomes that are not predetermined. • Complexity: Al problems typically involve a high level of complexity. • Uncertainty: Many Al problems involve uncertainty due to incomplete information, noisy data, or unpredictable environments. • Search and Optimization: Al problems often involve searching through large state spaces or optimizing certain parameters to find the best possible solution. • Knowledge Representation: Al problems require the system to represent knowledge in a form that can be used to make decisions or infer new information. • Learning and Adaptation: Al problems often involve systems that must learn from data or adapt their behavior over time based on feedback.

label: Problem Characteristics deck, slide 4
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Characteristics of Al Problem cont.. • Autonomy: Al systems often need to operate autonomously, making decisions or taking actions without direct human intervention. • Real-Time Decision Making: Many Al problems require real-time decision-making, where the system must quickly analyze data and make decisions within a constrained timeframe. • Goal-Oriented: Al problems are usually goal-oriented, meaning the system must achieve specific objectives or maximize certain rewards. • Handling of Natural Language: Some Al problems involve understanding, processing, or generating human language. These problems require the system to interpret text or speech and respond meaningfully. • Cognitive and Perceptual Abilities: Al problems often mimic human cognitive or perceptual abilities, such as reasoning, understanding, vision, and speech. • Heuristic Approach: Al problems often require heuristic methods, where the system uses "rules of thumb" or approximations to make decisions or find solutions, especially when exact solutions are not feasible due to the problem's complexity.

t: Search & Optimization Example: Google Maps Shortest Route Tool: Google Maps Demo Steps (Live in Class) 1. Open Google Maps. 2. Enter two locations, e.g.: • From: IILM University Gurugram • To: India Gate, New Delhi 3. Click "Directions. 4. Google Maps will display: • Multiple routes (fastest, shortest distance, traffic-optimized, toll-free, etc.). • Estimated travel time for each.

label: Problem Characteristics deck, slide 11

t: • Al Problem: "Find the best path among thousands of possible roads." • Search Space: All possible routes from Gurugram → Delhi. • Optimization Goal: Minimize travel time (not just distance). • Uncertainty Factor: Traffic, signals, road closures. • Al Technique Used: Google Maps uses Graph Search + Optimization algorithms (like Dijkstra's, A* search, and live traffic ML models). Note: • "Here, Google Maps doesn't just give one route. It gives optimized choices depending on what you want to minimize: time, distance, toll cost, or even fuel." • "This is a perfect example of an Al optimization problem. Just like chess Al explores many moves, Google Maps explores many routes, then optimizes." • "Notice that it doesn't guarantee a single best answer—it gives options, because conditions like traffic may change."

t: What is Problem Solving in Al • Problem solving in Artificial Intelligence (Al) refers to the process of designing systems that can find solutions to complex problems in a systematic, logical, or heuristic manner. • It is a key focus of Al and involves developing algorithms and techniques that allow machines to solve tasks that require human-like cognitive abilities such as reasoning, learning, and decision-making.

label: Problem Solving deck, slide 3
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Types of Problems in Al Al systems can face different types of problems. These problems are categorized based on their impact on the system's performance and how they can be handled: 1. Ignorable Problems These are minor issues that have little or no effect on the Al system's overall performance. They are often harmless and do not require immediate attention. Examples: • Small inaccuracies in predictions that don't affect the final result like a slight error in image classification. • Minor issues in data preprocessing that don't change the outcome. Handling: Ignored as they don't interfere with the system's primary function.

label: Problem Solving deck, slide 4
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: 2. Recoverable Problems Recoverable problems are those where the Al system encounters an issue but can be fixed with intervention either automatically or manually, such as error-handling functions. Examples: • Missing data that can be filled in using statistical methods. • System crashes that can be fixed by restoring from a backup. Handling: Requires action like automated error handling, retraining the model or system recovery through checkpoints.

label: Problem Solving deck, slide 5
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: 3. Irrecoverable Problems These are severe issues that cause permanent damage or failure, making it impossible for the system to recover. They can lead to significant performance loss. Examples: • Corrupted training data that causes bias and reduces the model's effectiveness. • Adversarial attacks that make the model untrustworthy. • Overfitting, where the model becomes too specialized and cannot adapt to new data. Handling: Requires a complete rebuild of the system including retraining the model or updating the data to eliminate underlying issues.

subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in Al Problem Solving • Problem Representation: • The first step in Al problem solving is to represent the problem in a way that a machine can process. This involves defining: - Initial state: Where the problem begins. - Goal state: The desired outcome. - Operators: The set of actions or transformations that can move from one state to another. - State space: All possible configurations of the problem between the initial and goal states.

label: Problem Solving deck, slide 12
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Techniques for Problem Solving in Al • Search Algorithms: Al problem solving often involves searching through a space of possible solutions to find the best or optimal one. Search algorithms are categorized as: - Uninformed Search (or Blind Search): These algorithms do not have additional information about the problem space. • Breadth-first search (BFS): Explores all nodes at the present depth level before moving on to nodes at the next depth level. • Depth-first search (DFS): Explores as far as possible down one branch before backtracking. - Informed Search (or Heuristic Search): These algorithms use domain-specific information (heuristics) to guide the search process. • Greedy Best-first search: Chooses paths that seem to lead directly to the goal based on a heuristic. • A*: A combination of the shortest path search and greedy search, balancing between the least cost and the heuristic.

label: Problem Solving deck, slide 13
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in Al Problem Solving • Heuristics: - Heuristics are strategies or rules of thumb that help make decisions or solve problems faster when exact solutions are computationally expensive or impossible. A heuristic function estimates the cost of reaching the goal from a given state. - Example: In a chess game, the number of pieces remaining on the board can be a heuristic to estimate the chances of winning.

Techniques include: Linear programming for solving problems involving linear relationships. 2. Dynamic programming for breaking down complex problems into smaller subproblems. Evolutionary algorithms like genetic algorithms that simulate natural selection to find optimal solutions.

Techniques like tokenization, Part-of-speech (PoS) and named entity recognition are important for chatbots, language translation and text summarization.

t: 8-Puzzle Problem he 8-Puzzle Problem is a classic Artificial Intelligence (Al) search problem used to demonstrate how an intelligent system can find a sequence of actions that transforms an initial state into a desired goal state. • What is the 8-Puzzle? The 8-puzzle consists of a 3 * 3 grid containing: • 8 numbered tiles (usually 1-8) • 1 empty space (blank) The objective is to move the tiles around until they match a predefined goal configuration. For example: Initial State 283 1 6 4 7 - 5 Goal State 123 8 4 765 The blank space _ can be moved up, down, left, or right, and a tile adjacent to the blank moves into the empty position.

t: Breadth-First Search • Overview: - BFS explores the search tree level by level, starting from the root node. It expands all nodes at a particular depth before moving to the next level. • How It Works: - Begin at the root node (or initial state). - Explore all neighboring nodes at the current depth level. - Move to the next level and repeat. • Characteristics: - Complete: Always finds a solution if one exists. - Optimal: Finds the shortest path (or least number of moves). • Example: - Solving a puzzle where all possible configurations are explored equally. • Drawback: - Memory-intensive, as it stores all nodes at each depth level.

t: Breadth First Search • Breadth First Search is a fundamental search algorithm that explores all possible paths level by level. It begins from the root node and explores all neighboring nodes before moving to the next level of nodes. BFS is complete and guarantees finding the shortest path if each move has the same cost. • However its main drawback is high memory usage as it stores all nodes at the current level before moving deeper which can grow rapidly for large or complex problems. • As BFS traverses the tree shallowest node first it would always pick the shallower branch until it reaches the solution or it runs out of nodes and goes to the next branch. • Path: S->D->G

t: Depth-First Search • Overview: - DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. • How It Works: - Start at the root node and go as deep as possible down one branch. If the end of the branch is reached, backtrack and explore the next branch. • Characteristics: - Less memory-intensive compared to BFS. May not be optimal and can get stuck in deep but wrong paths (infinite loops). • Example: - Navigating a maze by following one path until it ends, then backtracking if necessary.

You enter one corridor and keep walking until: • you reach the destination, or • you reach a dead end. Then you backtrack That is DFS. Data structure DFS uses: Stack - LIFO Last In → First Out.

t: Bidirectional Search This is a very interesting algorithm for classroom discussion. Instead of searching: START → → → → → GOAL search simultaneously from both ends: START → → → < + < GOAL When the two searches meet: Solution found! Example Finding a route between: Delhi → Mumbai One search starts from Delhi. Another starts from Mumbai. They try to meet somewhere in between. Why interesting? 0(b^(d/2)) rather than: Instead of searching an enormous tree of depth d, bidirectional search can potentially reduce the effective work dramatically, roughly toward: O(b^d) under ideal assumptions. Ask Why might searching from both directions be faster than searching from only one? Let students reason before explaining the branching-factor idea.

t: Local Search Algorithm • Search algorithms that operate using a single current state and move to neighboring states, often used for optimization problems. • Hill Climbing • Simulated Annealing • Applications: Optimizing circuit designs, machine learning model parameter tuning, and scheduling problems.

You can't see the whole mountain. You can only ask: "Which nearby position is higher?" You move there. Then ask again. That's hill climbing.

t: Real-Life Example of Hill Climbing Suppose a university wants to create the best timetable. You start with: Timetable A Make a small change: Move Data Science from Monday → Tuesday If the timetable becomes better: Keep the change. Then try another improvement. Eventually, you might reach a timetable where no small change improves it, even though a completely different timetable could be much better. That's a local optimum.

label: AI & Search Process deck, slide 49
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Simulated Annealing This is a fascinating one for students. Hill climbing says: "Never move downhill." Simulated annealing sometimes says: "I'll accept a worse solution temporarily if that helps me escape a bad local optimum." Real-life analogy Suppose you are searching for the best timetable. You find a reasonably good timetable. A small change makes it worse. Hill climbing says: X Reject it. Simulated annealing may say: Accept it temporarily. Why? Because the worse move may eventually lead to a much better region of the solution space.

label: AI & Search Process deck, slide 50
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Beam Search Beam Search keeps only a fixed number of promising candidates. Suppose: Beam width = 2 At every level, instead of keeping 20 possibilities, retain only the 2 most promising. Analogy Suppose 100 students participate in an initial competition. After Round 1: 100 → Top 10 Then: 10 → Top 3 Then: 3 → Winner You're reducing the search space aggressively. Advantage Fast and memory-efficient. Disadvantage You might discard the path that eventually contains the best solution.

t: Minimax Used for two-player games such as: • Tic-Tac-Toe • Chess • Checkers The Al assumes: "My opponent will also play intelligently." Suppose Al has two possible moves: AI /1 A // 5 23 4 Al wants the maximum outcome.

t: Alpha-Beta Pruning Minimax can become extremely expensive because game trees are huge. Alpha-beta pruning says: "If I already know that a branch cannot possibly improve my decision, why explore it?" It prunes unnecessary branches. Interesting analogy Suppose you're interviewing candidates. You already found someone with a score of 95. You interview another candidate and quickly determine their maximum possible score is 70. You don't need to spend another hour evaluating them. That's pruning. Important fact Alpha-beta pruning: • gives the same minimax result • but can examine far fewer nodes when ordering is favorable.

t: Monte Carlo Tree Search - MCTS This is another interesting modern search technique. Instead of exhaustively examining every possibility, MCTS performs simulations. Basic idea: Selection Expansion Simulation Backpropagation It became particularly famous through Al systems playing complex games such as Go. Real-life analogy Imagine choosing a restaurant. Instead of analyzing every restaurant in the city, you: • shortlist a few, • simulate/estimate likely experiences, • learn from repeated trials, • increasingly focus on promising options.

label: State Space deck, slide 2

t: What is State Space Search • State space search is a fundamental concept in artificial intelligence (Al) used to solve problems by exploring different states, of the problem until a solution is found. • The "state space" refers to the set of all possible states that can be reached from the initial state by applying various actions or operations. • The goal of state space search is to navigate through this space to find a path from an initial state to a goal state by using search algorithms.

label: State Space deck, slide 3
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • State: - A state represents a specific configuration of the problem at any given point in time. - The initial state is the starting point — The goal state is the desired outcome or solution.

label: State Space deck, slide 4
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • Operators: - Operators (or actions) are used to move from one state to another. - They define the possible transitions between states by applying some rules or actions. - For example, in a puzzle game, moving a tile is an operator that transitions from one board configuration (state) to another.

label: State Space deck, slide 5
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • State Space: - The state space is the entire set of all possible states that can be reached from the initial state by applying the available operators. - It can be visualized as a graph where nodes represent states, and edges represent transitions between states.

label: State Space deck, slide 6
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • Search Tree: - The search tree is a way to represent the exploration of the state space. - Each node in the tree represents a state, and branches represent the application of an operator to transition to a new state.

label: State Space deck, slide 7
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • Path: - A path in the state space is a sequence of states connected by operators, leading from the initial state to the goal state.

label: State Space deck, slide 8
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • Goal Test: - The goal test is a function that checks whether a given state is the goal state, i.e., if the desired solution has been found.

label: State Space deck, slide 9
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Concepts in State Space Search • Cost Function: - In some cases, moving from one state to another incurs a cost. - The cost function helps evaluate the efficiency of different paths and find the optimal solution in terms of the lowest cost.

label: State Space deck, slide 10
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Challenges in State Space Search • Combinatorial Explosion: The number of possible states can grow exponentially with the size of the problem, making exhaustive search impractical. • Efficiency: Finding optimal solutions in large state spaces requires efficient search algorithms that use heuristics or cost functions. • Memory Usage: Searches like BFS require significant memory, especially in large state spaces.

label: State Space deck, slide 11
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Applications of State Space Search • Path finding: Finding the shortest path in navigation or routing problems (e.g., GPS systems, robotics). • Game Solving: Exploring game states in chess, checkers, tic-tac-toe, etc. • Planning: Al agents use state space search for automated planning tasks (e.g., robot movement planning, scheduling). • Problem Solving: Solving puzzles like the 8-puzzle, Rubik's cube, or Sudoku using search techniques.

label: Turing Test deck, slide 7
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: How the Turing Test Works? • If the interrogator wouldn't able to distinguish the answers provided by both humans and computers then the computer passes the test and the machine(computer) is considered as intelligent as a human. • In other words, a computer would be considered intelligent if its conversation couldn't be easily distinguished from a human's. • The whole conversation would be limited to a text-only channel such as a computer keyboard and screen. B

label: Turing Test deck, slide 8
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Features of the Turing Test • Imitation Game: The judge is tasked with determining which participant is the machine by asking questions. Both the human and the machine respond, but the judge cannot see either and only evaluates based on their responses. • Focus on Behavior: The test does not measure whether the machine "thinks" like a human, but whether it can produce behavior indistinguishable from a human.

label: Turing Test deck, slide 9
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Significance of the Turing Test • Criterion for Al: The Turing Test was one of the first benchmarks proposed for assessing artificial intelligence. It highlights the notion of "intelligent behavior" rather than the internal workings of the machine. • Philosophical Implications: It raises important questions about the nature of intelligence, consciousness, and whether machines can truly think or simply simulate thinking.

label: Turing Test deck, slide 10
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Criticisms of the Turing Test • Limited Scope: Critics argue that the test only evaluates conversational ability and may not reflect true intelligence, as a machine might pass the test using clever tricks, without actually understanding the conversation. • Focus on Language: The test focuses on text-based communication, which might not capture the full range of human intelligence, such as creativity, emotions, or perception.

t: Four Principles of Human-Centered Design 1. People-Centered Core Definition: Start every design decision from real user needs, not assumptions. Key Concepts: • Empathy over Speculation: Designers must ground their choices in empirical user research (interviews, observation, contextual inquiry) rather than personal bias or unvalidated hypotheses. • Understanding Context: Focus on the real-world environment, constraints, physical capabilities, and emotional states of the people who will interact with the solution. Computational Design Thinking

label: CDT Unit 1 deck, slide 46
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Four Principles of Human-Centered Design 2. Radically Collaborative Core Definition: Bring diverse voices - users, experts, stakeholders - into the process. Key Concepts: • Cross-Disciplinary Synergy: Complex problems (especially computational and systemic ones) cannot be solved by a single perspective. • Co-Creation: Active participation of end-users, domain specialists, developers, business strategists, and edge-case stakeholders prevents blind spots and creates well-rounded solutions. Computational Design Thinking

label: CDT Unit 1 deck, slide 47

t: Four Principles of Human-Centered Design 2. Iterative & Experimental Core Definition: Prototype early, test often, and treat failure as useful data. Key Concepts: • Rapid Prototyping: Move quickly from abstract ideas to low-fidelity physical or digital representations (sketches, wireframes, paper models). • Feedback Loops: Continuous cycles of Build → Test → Learn refine solutions over time. • Reframing Failure: Unsuccessful experiments are not setbacks; they provide crucial data points that eliminate weak ideas early and cheap. Computational Design Thinking

t: Four Principles of Human-Centered Design 4. Optimistic & Creative Core Definition: Approach problems with confidence that a better solution exists. Key Concepts: • Growth Mindset: Assume that no matter how complex or "wicked" a problem seems, deliberate design methods can unlock meaningful improvements. • Divergent Thinking: Delay judgment during early stages to allow unconventional, high-potential ideas to surface before narrowing down. t: TOPIC 3| Why group brainstorming underperforms Production blocking Only one person can speak at a time. While you wait your turn, you rehearse - and forget - your own idea. Evaluation apprehension Fear of looking foolish in front of peers or seniors filters the boldest ideas before they are spoken. Anchoring & conformity The first idea voiced shapes everything after it. The group converges on one narrow direction. Social loafing In a group, individual effort is invisible, so some members quietly coast. Fix: generate alone first, combine as a group second. That is exactly what brainwriting does. Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation 12

t: TOPIC 5| Mind mapping for idea generation • A radial diagram: one central idea, branches outward, structure emerging as you go • One keyword per branch - phrases kill the associations a single word triggers • Thick branches near the centre, thinner as you move out: the hierarchy is visible • Use colour per branch and images where you can - recall improves sharply Never erase a branch while mapping. Sorting is a separate, later pass Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation Good for Unpacking a broad problem, grouping brainstorm output, revision notes, planning a project's scope Weak for Sequential processes, precise dependencies, anything needing exact ordering - use a flowchart instead 19

Each step must be correct, and you dig the same hole deeper. Excellent for solving - poor for finding. Lateral thinking Generative and provocative. Steps may be wrong' on the way. t: TOPIC 6 Four lateral thinking tools Random entry Pick a random word and force a connection to your problem. 'Umbrella' + attendance → shelter, cover, folds away, shared. Provocation (PO) State something deliberately impossible, then mine it. 'PO: the exam has no questions.' What would assessment become? 3 Challenge assumptions List everything that 'must' be true, then break each one. Must attendance be daily? Must it be per-class? Reversal Invert the goal. 'How do we make attendance as painful as possible?" Then reverse each answer into a fix. All four work by breaking the pattern your brain defaults to — that is the entire mechanism. Most will be nonsense. Two will not • Then reverse the goal: how would you design the worst possible version of this system? • Flip each of your 'worst' answers — that flipped list is a requirements document Debrief question: which forced connection surprised you, and what did it unlock? 7 MIN

t: TOPIC 7 • STAGE 1 Empathize - understand before you solve • Goal: see the problem as the user experiences it, not as you imagine it • Methods: interviews, shadowing, observation, immersion, diary studies • Ask about the last time it happened, not what people usually do - memory beats generalisation • Never ask leading questions or pitch your solution during an interview • Watch for workarounds - an improvised fix is a signal pointing straight at unmet need • Capture what you learn on an empathy map: says, thinks, does, feels SAYS quotes from the interview DOES observed actions & workarounds Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation USER THINKS beliefs, worries, hopes FEELS emotions and frustrations 26

t: TOPIC 7 • STAGE 2 Define — frame the problem sharply Point of View: [user] needs [need] because [ surprising insight ] "A first-year day scholar needs a way to prove she attended class, because her bus is late twice a week and the register closes before she arrives." A good problem statement is Human-centred • broad enough to allow several solutions • narrow enough to act on today • free of any implied solution Then reframe as How Might We 'How might we let students prove attendance without a fixed cut-off time?' - one HMW per insight, five or six per project Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation 27

t: TOPIC 7 • STAGE 3 Ideate - generate before you evaluate Set up One HMW question, a time box, a facilitator, and a visible wall or board for every idea. Generate Silent brainwriting first for volume, then a verbal round to build. Target a number, out loud. 3 Unstick When the pool goes flat, switch tool: SCAMPER on the strongest idea, or a random word. Cluster Group similar ideas, name each cluster. Structure appears without anyone judging yet. Non-negotiable: no evaluation of any kind until the generation time box has expired. Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation 28

t: TOPIC 8 From a pool to a shortlist cluster → dot-vote → score 100+ raw ideas 3-5 to build filters: desirable - feasible - viable • Cluster first, then choose - never rank a hundred loose sticky notes one by one • Score against criteria agreed before you look at the ideas, so the criteria cannot bend to a favourite • Three filters that survive contact with reality: desirable (users want it), feasible (we can build it), viable (it can be sustained) • Record why an idea was rejected - parked ideas often return when a constraint changes Unit 2 • Creative Thinking and Design Ideation 30

label: CDT Unit 2 deck, slide 30
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: TOPIC 8 Two fast selection tools Dot voting Each person gets a fixed number of dots (usually 3-5) and places them silently on the wall. Silent and simultaneous, so nobody anchors the room. Discuss only the top cluster afterwards. The NUF test Score each idea 1-10 on three axes: New — has it been tried here before? Useful — does it solve the real problem? Feasible - can we actually do it? Watch the pattern in NUF scores • High New, low Feasible → a research project, not this semester's build • High Feasible, low New → probably already exists; ask why it has not been done • High Useful, low New → boring and valuable. Often the correct choice Unit 2 • Creative Thinking and Design Ideation 31

t: TOPIC 8 The impact-effort matrix Plot every shortlisted idea on two axes only - impact on the user, effort to build • Quick wins first: they build momentum and evidence while costing little • Big bets need a plan, a budget and a sponsor - never start one by accident • Money pits get dropped early and explicitly, with the reason written down • Place ideas relative to each other, not on an absolute scale - comparison is the point Fastest way to turn a wall of sticky notes into a two-week plan. Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation QUICK WINS do first FILL-INS do if time allows EFFORT BIG BETS plan & resource MONEY PIT drop or defer 32

t: TOPIC 8 When the choice is contested: a weighted matrix Idea User impact x0.4 Feasibility x0.3 Novelty x0.2 Low cost x0.1 QR self check-in 8 9 4 8 Passive BLE attendance 9 4 9 5 Attendance streak dashboard 6 8 6 9 Score each idea 1-10 per criterion, multiply by the weight, sum. Agree the weights before scoring. • The three totals are close - that is information, not a tie. Close scores mean the criteria are not discriminating • Common traps: weights invented after scoring, one dominant voice scoring alone, criteria that all measure the same thing • The matrix does not make the decision. It makes the reasoning visible and arguable Unit 2 - Creative Thinking and Design Ideation Total 7.5 7.1 6.9 33

t: Algorithmic Thinking CORE IDEA "Algorithmic thinking is the ability to define a clear, ordered set of steps that solves a problem - so that anyone, or any machine, can follow it and get the same result." Precise Steps Every step is exact and unambiguous: nothing is left to guesswork. Repeatable The same steps give the same result every time they are followed. Transferable One solution can be reused for a whole class of similar problems. Computational Design Thinking 3

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 4
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: What Is an Algorithm? DEFINITION An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined instructions that takes some input, processes it, and produces the desired output. Input Data given to the algorithm Process Steps applied to the data Output The result produced The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century Persian mathematician. Computational Design Thinking Everyday algorithm: Making tea 1. Boil one cup of water 2. Add one teaspoon of tea leaves Simmer for 2 minutes 4. Add milk and sugar to taste 5. Boil for 1 more minute 6. Strain into a cup and serve

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 5
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Characteristics of Good Algorithms THE FIVE ESSENTIALS 1 2 3 4 5 Input Zero or more well-defined inputs G Output At least one result that answers the problem Definiteness Each step is clear and has only one meaning Finiteness Ends after a limited number of steps Effectiveness Every step is basic enough to actually carry out If any of these five is missing, the procedure is not a true algorithm. Quick check: is "search the library for a book" an algorithm? Not yet. It needs definite steps (which shelves, in what order) and a guaranteed stop (when the book is found or every shelf has been checked). Computational Design Thinking 5

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 6
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: The Five Characteristics Explained SIDE BY SIDE Characteristic Input Output Definiteness Finiteness Effectiveness What it means Clearly states what data it needs Produces a definite result Every instruction is precise Stops after a finite number of steps Each step can be done with basic operations Example of a violation "Calculate the bill" without saying which items A process that runs but never reports an answer "Add a little salt" or "wait a while" "Keep counting upwards" with no stopping rule "Pick the winning lottery number" Computational Design Thinking

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 7
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Beyond the Basics: Qualities of a Great Algorithm WHAT MAKES IT GOOD Correctness Gives the right output for every valid input. Efficiency Uses as little time and memory as possible. Readability Easy for others to understand and modify. Generality Works for a whole class of inputs, not one case. Robustness Handles unexpected or invalid input gracefully. Modularity Built from small parts that can be reused. Computational Design Thinking 7

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 8
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Pseudocode Writing CORE TOOL "Pseudocode is a plain-language description of an algorithm's steps, written in a structured, code-like style but free from the strict rules of any programming language." AE Language-Independent Can be translated into Python, C, Java or any other language. Plan Before Coding Lets you focus on logic first, syntax later. Easy to Share Teammates and non-programmers can review the logic. Computational Design Thinking 8

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 9
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Pseudocode Keywords and Conventions COMMON VOCABULARY Keyword BEGIN ... END INPUT / OUTPUT SET ... TO IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF WHILE ... DO ... ENDWHILE FOR ... TO ... ENDFOR Purpose Marks the start and end of the algorithm Read data in or display a result Assign a value to a variable Choose between paths (decision) Repeat while a condition is true Repeat a fixed number of times Convention: write keywords in CAPITALS and indent the steps inside every block. Computational Design Thinking Example BEGIN ... END INPUT marks OUTPUT total SET total TO 0 IF age >= 18 THEN ... WHILE count <= 10 DO ... FOR i FROM 1 TO 5 ...

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 10
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Pseudocode Example: Largest of Three Numbers WORKED EXAMPLE BEGIN INPUT a, b, c SET largest TO a IF b › largest THEN SET largest TO b ENDIE IF c > largest THEN SET largest TO c ENDIF OUTPUT • largest END Trace it with a = 12, b = 27, c = 9 Step Start Compare b Compare c Output Check assume a 27 > 12 V 9 > 27 X largest 12 27 27 27 Keep a "best so far" value and update it only when a bigger number appears. Computational Design Thinking 10

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 11
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Writing Good Pseudocode BEST PRACTICES Do • One action per line • Use meaningful names: total, not t • Indent steps inside IF and loops • Close every block (ENDIF, ENDWHILE) • Keep it detailed enough to code from Computational Design Thinking Avoid • Language-specific syntax like; or t} • Vague steps such as "process the data" • Mixing several actions in one line • Skipping the stopping condition of loops • Writing full program code 11

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 12
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Flowcharts CORE TOOL "A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm as standard symbols connected by arrows, making the flow of control visible at a glance." Visual Logic Decisions and loops are easy to see and follow. Easier Debugging Missing paths and dead ends stand out quickly. Clear Communication Works for technical and non-technical audiences. Computational Design Thinking 12

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 13
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Standard Flowchart Symbols VISUAL VOCABULARY Terminator Start or end of the flowchart Process A calculation or action, e.g. sum = a + b Input / Output Read data or display a result Decision A yes/no question that splits the flow Flow Line Shows the direction of control Connector Joins parts of a flowchart across a page Computational Design Thinking 13

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 14
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Flowchart Example: Is a Number Even or Odd? WORKED EXAMPLE Start Input N How to read it MOD gives the remainder after division. Decision: remainder 0 means even, otherwise odd. Both paths rejoin and reach one End. Yes No N MOD 2 = 0? Print "Even" Print "Odd" Trace: N = 7 7 MOD 2 = 1 → No → prints "Odd" End Computational Design Thinking 14

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 15
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Pseudocode vs. Flowchart SIDE BY SIDE Aspect Form Pseudocode Structured text Flowchart Diagram of symbols and arrows Showing overall flow and decisions Must be redrawn when logic changes Best for Ease of editing Large problems Audience Detailed logic, close to code Quick to change and extend Scales well to long algorithms Programmers and technical teams Becomes cluttered and hard to read Anyone, including non-programmers In practice they complement each other: sketch the flow, then refine it in pseudocode. Computational Design Thinking 15

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 16
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Problem Decomposition CORE IDEA "Decomposition means breaking a large, complex problem into smaller sub-problems that are each easy to understand, solve and test on their own." Manageable Pieces Small parts are less overwhelming than one big problem. Teamwork Different people can work on different parts at once. Tit Easier Testing Errors are found and fixed one part at a time. Computational Design Thinking 16

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 17
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Decomposition Example: Organizing a College Tech Fest WORKED EXAMPLE Organize the College Tech Fest Venue & Logistics Budget & Sponsors Events & Schedule Publicity • • • Book auditorium Arrange seating Set up AV and Wi-Fi • • • Estimate costs Approach sponsors Track spending • • • Choose competitions Invite judges Build timetable • • • Design posters Social media posts Open registrations Each leaf task is small enough to assign to one person and finish independently. Computational Design Thinking 17

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 18
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: How to Decompose a Problem STEP BY STEP 1 2 3 4 State the Goal Write down clearly what the full solution must achieve Split It Identify the main parts or stages of the problem Go Deeper Keep splitting until each part is simple to solve Solve & Combine Solve each part, then integrate and test the whole Rule of thumb: stop splitting when a sub-problem can be described in a single sentence and solved without further thought. Computational Design Thinking 18

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 19
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Pattern Recognition CORE IDEA Pattern recognition is spotting similarities, repetitions or trends within a problem, or between problems, so that one solution can be reused instead of solving each case from scratch. In Data Sales rise every festive season; spam emails share common words. In Steps The same calculation repeats for every student, item or day. Across Problems Finding the largest mark is like finding the cheapest flight. Computational Design Thinking 19

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 20
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Pattern Recognition in Action WORKED EXAMPLE 1. Spot the rule in a sequence 2. Spot repeated steps Computing results for 60 students: 3 6 9 12 ? Read marks Add them up Find percentage Pattern: each term is 3 more than the last Next term: 15 General rule: term n = 3 x n Pattern: identical steps for every student Solution: write the steps once and repeat them in a loop Computational Design Thinking 20

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 21
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Conditional Logic (If-Else) MAKING DECISIONS Conditional logic lets an algorithm choose different actions depending on whether a condition is true or false. IF Do something only when the condition is true. IF raining THEN take umbrella ENDIF IF - ELSE Choose one of two paths. IF marks >= 40 THEN OUTPUT "Pass" ELSE ENDIE OUTPUT "Fail" ELSE IF Ladder Choose one of many paths, checked in order. IF t > 35 THEN OUTPUT "Hot" ELSE IF t > 20 THEN OUTPUT "Warm" ELSE OUTPUT "Cold" ENDIF Computational Design Thinking 21

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 22
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: If-Else Example: Grade Calculator WORKED EXAMPLE BEGIN INPUT marks IF marks >= 90 THEN SET grade TO "A" ELSE IF marks >= 75 SET grade TO "B" ELSE IF marks >= 60 SET grade TO "C" ELSE IF marks >= 40 SET grade TO "D" ELSE SET "grade TO "F" ENDIF OUTPUT grade END Test cases THEN THEN THEN marks 95 82 61 40 33 First true condition marks >= 90 marks >= 75 marks >= 60 marks >= 40 none (ELSE) grade D F Order matters: check the highest range first. Once a condition is true, the rest are skipped. Computational Design Thinking 22

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 23
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Combining Conditions: AND, OR, NOT LOGICAL OPERATORS Truth table AND B True True A AND B True A OR B True NOT A False True False False True False OR False True False True True False False False False True AND needs both true • OR needs at least one • NOT flips the value NOT Computational Design Thinking Voting eligibility IF age >= 18 AND isCitizen THEN Weekend check IF day = "Sat" OR day = "Sun" THEN Login prompt IF NOT loggedIn THEN 23

t: Iterative Processes (Loops) REPEATING STEPS "A loop repeats a block of steps - either a fixed number of times or until a condition changes — so we write the steps once instead of over and over." FOR Loop Count-controlled: repeats a known number of times, e.g. print the 5-times table. WHILE Loop Condition-controlled: checks first, repeats while the condition is true. REPEAT-UNTIL Runs the body first, then checks, so it always executes at least once. Computational Design Thinking 24

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 25
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Anatomy of a Loop FOUR PARTS 1 Initialize Set the starting value 2 Condition Decide whether to continue BEGIN INPUT N SET sum TO 0 SET i TO 1 WHILE i <= N DO SET sum TO sum + i SET i TO i + 1 ENDWHILE OUTPUT sum END // initialize // condition I body // update Computational Design Thinking 3 Body The steps that repeat 4 Update Move towards the end Trace: N = 4 i 1 2 3 4 sum after body 1 3 6 10 i becomes 5, condition fails, output 10 25

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 26
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Choosing a Loop: FOR vs. WHILE COMPARISON FOR loop WHILE loop Use when the number of repetitions is known in advance Counter is managed for you Example: average marks of 60 students • Use when repetition depends on a condition You must update the condition yourself Example: ask for a password until it is correct FOR i FROM 1 TO 60 DO WHILE pwd <> stored DO Computational Design Thinking Infinite Loop Alert If the update step is missing, the condition never becomes false and the loop never ends. Always check that each pass moves closer to the stopping condition. 26

subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Basic Data Structures for Problem Solving CORE IDEA "A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data so that it can be accessed and changed efficiently. The right structure often makes the algorithm simple." Organize Data Group related values instead of using many separate variables. Fast Access Find, add or remove items quickly. Fit the Problem Each structure suits a different pattern of use. Computational Design Thinking 27

label: CDT Unit 3 deck, slide 28
subject: computational-design-thinking
t: Four Core Data Structures THE TOOLKIT Array / List Ordered items accessed by position (index). Like numbered seats in a classroom. marks 3] gives the 3rd mark. Queue (FIFO) First In, First Out: join at the back, leave from the front. Like a ticket counter line or a print queue. Computational Design Thinking Stack (LIFO) Last In, First Out: add and remove only from the top. Like a stack of plates, or the Undo button. Dictionary (Map) Stores key → value pairs for direct lookup. Like a phone book: name → number, roll no → student. 28

Searching a sorted list of 1,000,000 roll numbers in the worst case: 1,000,000 comparisons Linear search: check every item one by one 20 comparisons Binary search: halve the list at every step Time Complexity How the number of steps grows as input size n grows. Space Complexity How much extra memory the algorithm needs as n grows. Computational Design Thinking 30

t: Critical Thinking Fundamentals CORE IDEA "Critical thinking is the disciplined process of actively analyzing, evaluating and reasoning about information to reach a well-justified conclusion - rather than simply accepting it." Question Ask what is claimed, by whom, and on what basis. Evaluate Weigh evidence and reasoning, not opinions or popularity. Conclude Reach a justified judgement, and stay open to revising it. Computational Design Thinking 3

t: Critical vs. Uncritical Thinking FUNDAMENTALS Situation A viral message claims a new exam rule A friend recommends a laptop Code fails a test Uncritical thinker Critical thinker Forwards it immediately Checks the official university notice first Compares specs, reviews and price for own needs Two sources disagree Own idea is challenged Buys it on trust Blames the test or the compiler Picks the one they like Becomes defensive Reads the error and traces the cause step by step Compares evidence, date and authority of each Asks what evidence would change their mind Critical thinking is a habit of mind, not a talent: it improves with deliberate practice. t: Traits of a Critical Thinker FUNDAMENTALS ? Curious Asks "why?" and "how do we know?" before accepting a claim. Open-minded Considers other viewpoints and alternative explanations. 44 Fair-minded Judges arguments on merit, not on who is making them. Logical Checks that conclusions really follow from the reasons. Computational Design Thinking Sceptical Asks for evidence; does not accept claims at face value. Reflective Reviews own thinking and corrects mistakes.

subject: computational-design-thinking

Purpose What is the goal? Question What problem are we solving? Information What data and facts are used? Inferences What conclusions are drawn? 5 Concepts What ideas or theories apply? Assumptions What is taken for granted? Implications What follows if we accept this? 8 Point of view From whose perspective? Computational Design Thinking 6

How can we check? Can you be more specific? Breadth Logic Does it address the complexities? Have other viewpoints been considered? Does the conclusion follow? Relevance How does it relate to the question? Significance Fairness Is this the most important point? Is anyone's interest ignored or misrepresented? Elements tell you what to examine; standards tell you how well it has been done. Computational Design Thinking

t: Reasoning in Action: Worked Examples DEDUCTIVE VS. INDUCTIVE Deductive P1 All registered students can use the library. P2 Riya is a registered student. C Therefore, Riya can use the library. Inductive P1 The canteen was crowded at 1 PM on Monday. P2 It was crowded at 1 PM on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. C So it will probably be crowded at 1 PM on Friday. Valid: the conclusion is guaranteed. Sound: valid AND the premises are actually true. Strong: the premises make the conclusion likely. A single quiet Friday would not disprove the pattern, but it would weaken it. Computational Design Thinking 10

t: Syllogisms: The Structure of a Deductive Argument SYLLOGISMS A syllogism draws a conclusion from two premises that share a common term. Major premise All programmers are problem-solvers. Minor premise Aman is a programmer. Conclusion Therefore, Aman is a problem-solver. Major term Predicate of the conclusion: problem-solver Minor term Subject of the conclusion: Aman Middle term Links the premises, absent from conclusion: programmer Computational Design Thinking 12

t: Three Types of Syllogism SYLLOGISMS Categorical Uses "all", "some", "no". All mammals are warm-blooded. All whales are mammals. .. All whales are warm-blooded. Hypothetical Uses "if ... then". If it rains, the match is cancelled. It is raining. •• The match is cancelled. Disjunctive Uses "either ... or". The bug is in the front end or the back end. It is not in the front end. . • It is in the back end. Hypothetical forms: modus ponens (if P then Q; P; so Q) is valid. Modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; so not P) is valid. Affirming the consequent (if P then Q; Q; so P) is a fallacy. Computational Design Thinking 13

t: Cause-and-Effect Analysis FINDING REAL CAUSES Cause-and-effect analysis looks for the root reason behind a problem, instead of treating its symptoms. Correlation Two things change together. Ice-cream sales and drowning cases both rise in summer, but one does not cause the other: hot weather drives both. Causation One thing actually produces the other. Removing the cause removes or reduces the effect, and the cause comes before the effect. Before claiming "A causes B", check: 1. Does A happen before B? 2. Is the link consistent and repeatable? 3. Is there a plausible mechanism? 4. Have other causes (a hidden third factor) been ruled out? Computational Design Thinking 21

t: WELCOME Why Engineers Need This Course Engineering training teaches you to solve well-defined problems. Entrepreneurship asks a harder question: which problems are worth solving, for whom, and how do you know? See opportunity, not just specs Move from "build what's requested" to "spot what's needed." 4 Think in prototypes, not perfection Test small, cheap versions of ideas before over-engineering them. Bridge technical and human value Connect what you can build to what people will actually use and pay for. Engineers are trained to make things work. Entrepreneurship is learning to ask whether they're worth making at all. Guiding idea for this course This first session lays the groundwork: what innovation actually means, how it differs from invention, and the mindset that connects the two to entrepreneurship. 03

label: EM orientation deck, slide 4
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: CORE CONCEPT What Is Innovation? Innovation is the successful introduction of something new - an idea, product, process, or business model - that creates value for someone. Being "new" isn't enough; it has to actually get used and matter. Product A new or improved offering Process A better way of doing existing work Business Model A new way of creating and capturing value Market An existing offering reaching a new audience The engineer's role in innovation Engineers are often the ones who make innovation technically possible - but technical possibility alone doesn't guarantee value. The rest of this course is about closing that gap between "can build it" and "should build it." 04

t: INNOVATION VS. INVENTION Two Words Often Confused Every innovation may start with an invention - but most inventions never become innovations. Invention Innovation The creation of something new - a device, method, or idea — that did not exist before. It is a technical or creative act. Taking an idea - invented or existing - and turning it into something that creates real value and gets adopted. - Focused on novelty - Focused on adoption and value - Often happens in a lab or workshop - Happens in the market, with real users - Success = "does it work?" - Success = "does it get used?" - Can sit unused for decades - Requires a business model, not just a mechanism 05

Ask: who needs this, will they adopt it, and does it survive contact with the market? 3 Most real projects need both Great engineers know when to switch from "make it work" to "make it matter." 08

t: ENTREPRENEURIAL MINDSET What Does This Mean for an Engineer? An entrepreneurial mindset doesn't mean every engineer must start a company. It means approaching technical work with the same instincts a founder brings to a business: curiosity about unmet needs, comfort with uncertainty, and a bias toward testing ideas in the real world. Traditional Engineering Focus - Given a spec, build to it precisely Entrepreneurial Engineering Focus - Questions whether the spec solves a real problem - Optimize for correctness and reliability - Optimizes for validated value, then reliability - Success measured by technical performance - Success measured by adoption and impact 09

t: FOUNDATIONS What is Design Thinking? DEFINITION A human-centered approach to innovation that puts real people's needs first, reframes problems as opportunities, and rapidly tests ideas before committing to them. "Desirable, feasible, and viable" — the sweet spot every solution aims for. Design Thinking • Problem to Solution P P P People • Desirability Deeply understand users through empathy and observation. Process • Feasibility Iterate quickly - build, test, learn, and refine. Purpose • Viability Deliver value that is sustainable for the business. 03

t: SECTION 01 The Design Thinking Framework Five non-linear stages - teams loop back as they learn. 1 2 3 4 5 Empathize Understand users' needs, emotions and context. Define Synthesize insights into a clear problem statement. Ideate Generate a wide range of possible solutions. Prototype Build quick, low-cost representations of ideas. Test Try prototypes with users and gather feedback. Iterative loop: insights from Test feed back into Define and Ideate — the process is a cycle, not a straight line. t: SECTION 01 • HOW IT WORKS Diverge, then Converge Each stage is either about opening up options or narrowing them down. DIVERGE Expand possibilities • Empathize - gather many perspectives • Ideate - generate lots of ideas • Prototype - explore multiple concepts Go wide: defer judgment, seek quantity and variety. Design Thinking • Problem to Solution CONVERGE Make focused choices • Define — one sharp problem statement • Select - cluster and prioritize ideas • Test - validate and decide what stays Go narrow: analyze, prioritize, and commit. 05

t: SECTION 02 Problem Identification Solving the right problem matters more than solving a problem right. Most failed products are well-built answers to the wrong question. Symptom vs. root cause — look past what's visible to what's causing it. • User's problem, not yours — frame it from the user's perspective. • Evidence over assumption - ground the problem in observation and data. Narrow and specific - a focused problem is a solvable problem. Design Thinking • Problem to Solution WHY IT MATTERS ~35% 5x 1 of startups fail because there was no real market need. cheaper to fix a problem framed correctly up front than after build. sharp problem statement aligns the entire team. 06

label: EM Unit 2 deck, slide 7

t: SECTION 02 • TOOLKIT Techniques to Frame the Problem 5 Whys 1 Ask "why?" repeatedly to drill from symptom to root cause. e.g. Why is checkout slow? → ... → the API retries 3x on timeout. How Might We Turn a pain point into an open, optimistic design question. e.g. "How might we make first-time setup feel effortless?" Point-of-View Problem Statement 3 4 State user + need + insight in a single guiding sentence. A concise, testable definition of the problem and its scope. e.g. "A busy nurse needs fast handoffs because errors cost lives." e. g. "Users abandon onboarding at step 3 due to unclear input rules." Design Thinking • Problem to Solution 07

t: SECTION 03 Problem-Solution Fit The point where a validated problem meets a solution that genuinely resolves it for a defined group of users. It comes BEFORE product-market fit. • Real, urgent problem - people already seek workarounds. • Clear target segment - you know exactly whose problem it is. • Solution resolves it - measurably better than the alternatives. Design Thinking - Problem to Solution PROBLEM validated FIT SOLUTION that works 08

t: SECTION 03 • VALIDATION How to Validate the Fit 1 2 3 4 Define the segment Confirm the pain Map the solution Test with a signal Name the specific customers who feel the pain most acutely. Interview users; look for existing workarounds and willingness to pay. Sketch how your solution removes the pain, end to end. Landing page, prototype or concierge MVP to measure real interest. Signal to look for: users are disappointed when they can't use your solution. 5 Measure & decide Track adoption, retention and satisfaction - pivot or persevere. 09

Seven prompts to transform an existing idea. • Go for quantity • Build on others • Defer criticism • Substitute • Combine • Adapt • Modify • Eliminate • Reverse Design Thinking • Problem to Solution Mind Mapping Branch outward from a central theme visually. • One central node • Radiating branches • Words + images 10

t: SECTION 04 • TECHNIQUE 1 Brainstorming THE GROUND RULES Defer judgment — no idea is criticized during the session. Encourage wild ideas - the bolder the better; edit later. • Go for quantity - more ideas raise the odds of a great one. • Build on ideas — use "yes, and.." to extend others. Stay focused - keep to the topic / the How-Might-We question. • One conversation - let each idea be heard, no side-talk. Be visual - sketch and write ideas where all can see. Design Thinking • Problem to Solution RUNNING A SESSION Frame - Open with a clear How-Might-We question. Diverge - Silent solo ideation, then share out loud. 3 Cluster - Group similar ideas into themes. Vote - Dot-vote to surface the strongest ideas. 4 Refine - Develop top picks into concepts. 5 11

Merge two ideas, steps or features. A Adjust an idea from another context. M Magnify, minify or reshape an element. Put to other use Eliminate P Apply it to a new purpose or market. t: Introduction to Venture Modelling UNIT IV Definition Building a simple, testable picture of how a startup will create, deliver and capture value - and listing the assumptions that must be true for it to work. How to apply List assumptions → rank by risk → draw a one-page model (canvas + unit economics) → test the riskiest assumption cheaply → update the model with evidence. Value creation Who is the customer? What problem do they have? Why is our solution better than today's workaround? Value delivery Which channels, operations, partners and resources are needed to serve customers reliably? Value capture Pricing, revenue streams, cost structure and margin - how does the venture earn more than it spends? Evidence loop Assumption → experiment → data → decision: pivot, persevere or stop. Mini-model: price R500 - variable cost 7300 = contribution Z200 per order. Fixed cost *2,00,000 per month ÷ *200 = break-even at 1,000 orders a month. Common health check: lifetime value ÷ customer-acquisition cost LTV: CAC of about 3 or more. Takeaway: A model is a set of testable guesses. Find the fatal assumption early and cheaply — don't try to forecast perfectly. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 4
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Venture Modelling - Three Examples UNIT IV Dropbox USA • 2007 • testing demand Situation File syncing was hard to explain and hard to build. Would anyone actually want it? Zerodha India • founded 2010 • unit economics Situation Traditional brokers charged a percentage of each trade, so retail traders paid more as trades grew. Tata Nano India • 2008-2019 • a cautionary model Situation Tata aimed at a R1 lakh car for families riding two- wheelers, working backwards from the price. What they did Drew Houston made a short demo video showing the product working and shared it with early- adopter communities (Digg, Hacker News). The beta waitlist jumped from about 5,000 to 75,000 overnight - before the full product existed. What they did Zerodha modelled a flat fee: 720 per executed order or 0.03%, whichever is lower, with no brokerage on equity delivery. A 750,000 trade pays 715; a 11,00,000 trade pays R20. It grew without venture funding. What they did The plant moved from Singur to Sanand in 2008, delaying the 2009 launch. The car was widely seen as "the cheapest car", a status stigma for aspirational buyers. Sales stayed below plan and production wound down by 2019. Teaching point Model and test the riskiest assumption (demand) first. A video tested it at almost zero cost. Teaching point Unit economics decide the model: low cost to serve each trade allowed a low flat price that still scaled. Teaching point A cost model can be right while the business fails. Test demand and brand assumptions too, not only cost. Takeaway: Dropbox tested demand, Zerodha designed unit economics, Nano shows what happens when an assumption (status) is never tested. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 5
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Value Proposition Canvas UNIT IV Definition A tool that matches what customers need - their jobs, pains and gains — with what you offer, so the two "fit". (Osterwalder & Pigneur) How to apply Fill the customer profile first from interviews → rank pains and gains by importance → design the value map for the top ones → test the fit with evidence. VALUE MAP - what you offer CUSTOMER PROFILE - what they need Products & services What we offer, e.g. app, device, service Jobs What the customer is trying to get done FIT Pain relievers How we remove or reduce customer pains Pains Obstacles, risks, costs, frustrations Gain creators How we create benefits customers want Gains Outcomes and benefits they want Takeaway: Start from the customer's job, not your feature list. Fit exists only when evidence shows customers care about the pains you relieve. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 6
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Value Proposition - Three Examples UNIT IV Meesho India • reseller platform Situation Homemakers, students and small entrepreneurs wanted income from home but lacked capital, stock and shipping know-how. What they did Job: earn income from home. Pains: no capital, unsold stock, shipping hassle. Meesho's fit: share a ready catalogue on WhatsApp or Facebook, hold no inventory, Meesho packs and ships, the reseller keeps the margin. Practo India • founded 2008 • healthcare Situation Patients struggled to find a trusted doctor, check availability and avoid long clinic queues. Aravind Eye Care India • founded 1976 • social value Situation Cataract blindness was common, but surgery was costly and hospitals were far from villages. What they did Job: reach the right doctor quickly. Pains: unclear availability, unverified information, waiting. Practo's relievers: search by speciality and location, doctor profiles with patient reviews, instant booking and online consultations. What they did Job: restore sight. Pains: cost, distance, lost wages. Relievers: tiered pricing where patients choose free, subsidised or paid care; eye camps that bring screening to villages; high-volume standardised surgery. Over half of patients pay nothing or subsidised rates. Teaching point Strong fit: every top pain (capital, inventory, logistics) has a direct pain reliever. Teaching point Trust is a gain creator: reviews and verified profiles solved an information pain, not just a booking pain. Teaching point Paying patients cross-subsidise others while quality stays the same: fit can combine social and financial value. Takeaway: In each case the venture named a specific customer job and pain first - then designed the offer to match. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 7
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Business Model Canvas UNIT IV Definition A one-page map of nine building blocks showing how an organisation creates, delivers and captures value. (Osterwalder & Pigneur) How to apply Start with Customer Segments and Value Proposition → fill the other blocks → check revenue exceeds cost → test each block with evidence. Key Partners Who are our key partners and suppliers? What do they provide? Key Activities What must we do best? (build, platform, logistics) Value Propositions What value do we deliver? Which customer problem do we solve? Which needs do we satisfy? Customer Relationships How do we get, keep and grow customers? Customer Segments Who are we creating value for? Who is the most important customer? Key Resources Which assets do we need? (people, IP, tech, cash) Channels How do we reach customers? (app, stores, partners) Cost Structure What are the biggest fixed and variable costs? Which blocks cost the most? Revenue Streams What do customers really pay for, how do they pay, and how much? Takeaway: Read the canvas as a story: partners and activities build the value, channels deliver it, and revenue must exceed cost. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 7

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 8
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Business Model Canvas - Three Examples UNIT IV Zomato (now Eternal) India • two-sided marketplace Situation A marketplace connecting diners, restaurants and delivery partners. What they did Segments: diners and restaurants. Value: discovery, ordering, fast delivery. Revenue: commissions, ads, delivery and platform fees, Gold membership. Key resources: app, restaurant network, rider fleet. Costs: rider payouts, tech, discounts, marketing. Amul India • farmer cooperative • 1946 Situation Farmer-owned cooperative built to give small dairy farmers a fair, assured market. Freshworks India/USA • SaaS • Nasdaq 2021 Situation Small and mid-size firms wanted easy, affordable support software, not heavy enterprise tools. What they did Partners: village dairy societies → district unions → state federation (GCMMF). Value: affordable, trusted dairy products and a fair price for farmers. Revenue: sale of milk, butter, cheese, ice cream. Costs: milk procurement, processing, cold chain. What they did Segments: small and mid-size businesses, then larger teams. Value: easy-to-adopt cloud software for support, sales and IT. Revenue: tiered subscriptions, with free plans and trials to attract users. Costs: R&D, cloud hosting, sales and marketing. Teaching point Each revenue stream is tied to a different segment; a marketplace must keep both sides happy. Teaching point Key Partners can be the core of a model: here farmers are both suppliers and owners. Teaching point Subscriptions give recurring revenue; low-friction sign-up (free plan) acts as the main channel. Takeaway: Three different models - marketplace, cooperative, SaaS - yet the same nine blocks describe all of them. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 9
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Customer Segments, Revenue & Cost Structure UNIT IV Definition Segments say who pays; revenue streams say how they pay; the cost structure says what it costs to serve them. Together they decide profitability. How to apply Choose a first (beachhead segment → price against the value it gets → list every cost → compute unit economics → test willingness to pay. Customer segments • Mass market - one broad need (Jio) • Niche - a specific need • Segmented - groups with different needs • Multi-sided - linked groups (Zomato) • Start with a small, reachable segment in urgent pain Revenue streams • Product sale (Lenskart) • Subscription (Freshworks) • Transaction fee (Razorpay) • Commission (Zomato) • Advertising (Meesho sellers) • Freemium, licensing, leasing Cost structure • Fixed: salaries, rent, tech • Variable: materials, delivery, payment fees • CAC: cost to acquire a customer • Cost-driven vs value-driven models • Scale lowers cost per unit Contribution margin = price - variable cost • Break-even units = fixed cost ÷ contribution margin • Healthy LTV: CAC = 3 or more Takeaway: A venture is only viable when revenue per customer, minus the cost to serve and acquire them, stays positive at scale. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 10
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Segments, Revenue & Cost - Three Examples UNIT IV Reliance Jio India • 2016 • mass-market segment Situation In 2016 most Indians paid high prices for mobile data, and voice was the main product. What they did Segment: mass-market mobile users. Free launch offers, then low-priced prepaid data plans (Jio Prime: 799 once plus a 7303 monthly plan in 2017). Huge upfront network investment spread over volume. It reached 100 million users in 170 days. Lenskart India • founded 2010 • cost structure Situation Buying spectacles meant slow, high-margin local shops with limited choice. What they did Segment: spectacle and contact-lens users, from urban youth to smaller cities. Revenue: sale of frames, lenses and contact lenses. Costs are managed by designing and making products in- house and selling through its own app, website and many stores, with eye tests in stores and at home. Razorpay India • founded 2014 • B2B Situation Online businesses needed an easy way to accept UPI, cards and net banking without building bank integrations. What they did Segment: businesses from startups to large enterprises. Revenue: a small percentage fee on each successful payment, plus add-ons such as business banking and lending. Costs: bank and network fees, security, compliance and engineering. Teaching point A very high fixed cost works only with huge volume: price low, scale fast, cut cost per user. Teaching point Controlling the supply chain (vertical integration) lowers variable cost and funds a low price. Teaching point Transaction-fee revenue grows with customers success, but margin depends on costs passed through by banks. Takeaway: Jio chose volume, Lenskart controls cost, Razorpay earns per transaction - each pairs a segment with a fitting money model. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 10
