t: IP Basics for Startups UNIT IV Definition Intellectual property (IP) is legal ownership of creations of the mind — inventions, brands, designs, creative works and know-how - so others cannot copy them. How to apply Identify what is truly valuable → pick the right IP type → file before any public disclosure → sign NDAs and IP-assignment agreements with founders, staff and vendors. IP type Patent Trademark Copyright Design Geographical Indication Trade secret What it protects New, inventive, industrially useful inventions Brand names, logos, slogans Original works: software code, content, music Shape or look of a product Products tied to a region Confidential formulas and know-how Duration in India 20 years from filing 10 years, renewable Author's life + 60 years 10 years, +5 extension 10 years, renewable No registration; lasts while secret Startup India support DPIIT-recognised startups get an 80% rebate on patent filing fees, a 50% rebate on trademark fees, and fast-track patent examination. Panels of IP facilitators give free general advice. Takeaway: IP is a business asset: choose it deliberately, file early, protect it by contract — and never infringe someone else's. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 11

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 12
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: IP - Three Examples UNIT IV Turmeric patent India vs USA • patent • prior art Situation In 1995 the US granted a patent (No. 5,401,504) for using turmeric to heal wounds — a use known in India for centuries. What they did India's CSIR challenged it with old Sanskrit texts and an Indian journal article as prior art. The US Patent Office revoked the patent in 1997. India later built the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) so examiners can find such prior art. Darjeeling Tea India • geographical indication Situation A famous regional name can be misused by sellers whose product is not from that region. Coca-Cola formula USA • trade secret Situation A secret recipe is valuable only if it stays secret; a patent would expire and require public disclosure. What they did The Tea Board of India registered Darjeeling tea in 2004-05 as India's first Gl under the GI Act, 1999. Only tea grown and processed in the defined hill gardens may carry the name, and the Tea Board licenses the logo. What they did Coca-Cola has never patented its formula, in use since 1886. It guards it as a trade secret through restricted knowledge, confidentiality agreements and secure storage, while the brand is protected separately as a trademark. Teaching point A patent needs novelty. Prior art, even old local knowledge, can invalidate it - search before you file. Teaching point A GI protects a shared regional name for a community of producers - ideal for crafts, foods and farm products. Teaching point Choose IP by goal: patents give a time-limited monopoly in return for disclosure; secrets last only while secret. Takeaway: Patent, GI and trade secret protect different things — matching the right tool to the asset is the skill. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 12

subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Ethics in Entrepreneurship UNIT IV Definition Making decisions that are honest, fair and responsible to all stakeholders - customers, employees, investors, partners and society - even when the law does not force you to. How to apply Write a code of conduct → test big decisions with the "front-page test" → keep accurate records → protect user data → give people a safe way to raise concerns. Honesty No inflated metrics, false claims or hidden risks when talking to investors or customers. Safety & quality Do not ship products that can harm. If something goes wrong, act and recall quickly. Data privacy Collect only what you need, with consent. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets duties for handling personal data. Governance & fairness Accurate accounts, no conflicts of interest, fair treatment of staff, vendors and partners. Takeaway: Legal is the minimum. Trust is a startup's most valuable asset: slow to build, fast to lose. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 13

label: EM Units 4–5 deck, slide 14
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Ethics - Three Examples UNIT IV Theranos USA • health • failure of honesty Situation A health startup founded in 2003 claimed a few drops of blood from a finger-prick could run many lab tests. What they did Its devices could not deliver what was claimed, yet investors and partners were shown inflated results. A 2015 news investigation exposed this and the company closed in 2018. Founder Elizabeth Holmes was convicted in 2022 of defrauding investors and sentenced to over 11 years. Johnson & Johnson USA • 1982 • ethical crisis response Situation Seven people in Chicago died after taking Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with cyanide. What they did J&J put public safety first: it warned the public, recalled about 31 million bottles, and later introduced tamper-resistant packaging - though it was not responsible for the tampering. Customer trust and sales recovered. Satyam Computers India • 2009 • failure of governance Situation Satyam was one of India's best-known IT firms, listed on stock exchanges and trusted by global clients. What they did In January 2009 chairman B. Ramalinga Raju admitted to inflating profits and cash balances by about 77,000 crore over several years. The company nearly collapsed and was rescued by Tech Mahindra; Raju was convicted in 2015. Teaching point Overclaiming is fraud, not "fake it till you make it". In health, false results can cost lives. Teaching point Act fast, put customers ahead of short-term profit and communicate openly in a crisis. Teaching point False accounts and weak governance destroy value for employees, investors and the brand. Takeaway: Theranos lied, J&J protected customers, Satyam falsified accounts — ethics decides whether trust survives a crisis. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 14

subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Sustainability for Startups UNIT IV Definition Building ventures that create economic value while reducing harm to — and ideally benefiting - people and the planet: the "triple bottom line" of profit, people and planet. How to apply Map environmental and social impact along your value chain → pick one or two measurable targets → redesign materials, energy and waste → test whether customers pay or costs fall. Reduce Use less energy, water and material in making and delivering the product. Reuse & recycle Circular models keep materials in use instead of dumping them as waste. Include Fair pay, local sourcing and access for under-served people and farmers. Measure & report Claims need data. Avoid "greenwashing" - green messages without proof. Links to the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as 7 Clean energy, 8 Decent work, 9 Industry & innovation, 12 Responsible consumption, 13 Climate action. Takeaway: Sustainability is strongest when it lowers cost or opens a new market - not when it is added as decoration. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 15

subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Sustainability - Three Examples UNIT IV Bakeys Foods India • Hyderabad • founded 2011 Situation Huge numbers of plastic spoons are thrown away every day, adding to waste and landfill. What they did Narayana Peesapaty, a former ICRISAT scientist, started Bakeys to make edible spoons from sorghum (jowar, rice and wheat. Sorghum is a hardy crop needing little water, and a discarded spoon decomposes within days. Patagonia USA • outdoor clothing • business model Situation An outdoor-clothing company whose founder believed business should help protect the environment. What they did Patagonia pledges 1% of sales to environmental causes and repairs and resells used clothing. In 2022 founder Yvon Chouinard transferred ownership to a trust and a non-profit, so profits not reinvested go to fight climate change. Cochin Intl. Airport India • Kerala • solar power Situation Airports use large amounts of electricity, a big recurring cost. What they did Cochin International Airport Ltd built a large solar plant on its land and in 2015 became the world's first fully solar-powered airport. It received the UN's Champions of the Earth award in 2018. Solar cut its electricity bills as well as emissions. Teaching point The hurdle: in 2016 an edible spoon cost about twice a plastic one. Green products must close the price gap or find premium buyers. Teaching point Sustainability can shape ownership and the business model itself, not only the product. Teaching point Green investment can pay back: a one-time capital cost reduced a recurring cost. Always build a business case. Takeaway: A product, a business model, and an infrastructure choice - sustainability works at every level, and must still make financial sense. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 16

t: Introduction to Startup Pitching UNIT V Definition A short, structured, persuasive presentation that helps a specific audience make a specific decision - to fund, partner, buy, join or award you. How to apply Know the audience and the decision you want → build a story: hook, problem, solution, proof, ask → rehearse to time → answer questions honestly. Type of pitch Elevator pitch Demo day pitch Competition / hackathon Investor pitch Sales pitch Length 30-60 seconds 2-3 minutes 5-7 minutes 10-20 min + Q&A Varies Goal Earn a follow-up conversation Get investor meetings Win the award and visibility Win funding Win a customer Questions every audience asks Why this problem? Why you? Why now? What is the proof? What do you need from us? Takeaway: A pitch is not a product tour. It is a short argument backed by evidence, ending in a clear ask. t: Startup Pitching - Three Examples UNIT V Apple iPhone launch USA • Jan 2007 • mass-audience pitch Situation Phones, music players and internet devices were three separate products for most people. Y Combinator Demo Day USA • Winter 2015 • investor pitch Situation 114 startups had to pitch to a room of investors in a single batch - the largest YC had held to that point. Shark Tank India India • Season 1 • televised pitch Situation Season 1 (Dec 2021-Feb 2022) drew about 62,000 aspirants; 198 businesses pitched to the "Sharks". What they did Steve Jobs announced "three revolutionary products": a widescreen iPod, a phone and an internet communicator - repeating them until the audience realised it was one device. He then demonstrated it live on stage. What they did Each founder had roughly two and a half minutes. Typical content: the problem, the solution, growth numbers and team, ending with a line repeating what the company does. Founders rehearsed with YC partners beforehand. What they did Each founder states an ask - money for equity - which implies a valuation: R50 lakh for 5% means 710 crore. The Sharks probe margins, customer- acquisition cost, repeat sales and defensibility, then bargain or decline. Teaching point One simple idea, repetition and a live demo can make a complex product instantly understandable. Teaching point In a very short slot, clarity beats completeness: investors only decide whether to take a follow-up meeting. Teaching point Know your numbers and valuation logic; credibility is won or lost in the Q&A. Takeaway: Three audiences, three formats - the pitch changes with the audience, but a clear idea and proof never do. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 18

t: Elements of an Effective Pitch Deck UNIT V Definition A short slide presentation that tells investors the story of the business: problem, solution, market, model, proof, team and ask. How to apply Write the one-sentence story first → give each slide one headline → add one proof point (data, quote, demo) per slide → cut anything that does not support the ask. 1 Title & hook What do you do, in one line? 2 Problem Whose pain, and how big? 3 Solution How do you fix it? 4 Product / demo What does it look like? 5 Market size How big can it get? 6 Business model How do you make money? 7 Traction What proof already exists? 8 Competition & moat Why will you win? 9 Team Why are you the ones? 10 Ask & use of funds What do you need, for which milestones? Rules of thumb: 10-12 slides • one idea per slide • large fonts (Kawasaki: 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point) • numbers over adjectives Takeaway: Each slide answers one investor question. If a slide does not help the decision, cut it. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 19

t: Pitch Decks - Three Examples UNIT V Airbnb (2009) USA • about 10 slides • seed deck Situation Founders Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia and Nathan Blecharczyk needed seed money for a new idea: renting spare rooms. What they did About ten slides: the cover line "Book rooms with locals, rather than hotels"; problem; solution; validation using Couchsurfing and Craigslist; market size; product; model — a 10% commission; competition; team. It helped raise about $600K, including from Sequoia Capital. Uber (UberCab, 2008) USA • 25 slides • $200K pre-seed Situation Garrett Camp's team pitched a members-only premium car service booked from a phone, first called UberCab. What they did A 25-slide deck (published by Camp in 2017) covered the taxi problem, the app, the fleet, target cities and market size - about $4.2B for the US taxi and limo industry. It raised a $200K pre-seed. Analysts note it was long and its story jumped around. Buffer (2011) USA • public seed deck Situation After raising a seed round of about $500K, co- founder Joel Gascoigne shared the deck publicly. What they did The deck was built around transparent metrics - real traction data rather than projections - plus the team and the ask. Because it was shared openly, it became one of the most studied seed decks for software startups. Teaching point Simple order, one idea per slide, and a business model that fits in a single sentence. Teaching point Facts are not enough: order slides so each leads to the next, and include a "why now" (smartphones). Teaching point Early traction data builds more credibility than a bigger market-size claim. Takeaway: Airbnb shows simplicity, Uber shows the cost of a loose narrative, Buffer shows the power of real numbers. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 20

t: Storytelling for Startups UNIT V Definition Turning facts into a memorable narrative with a character, a problem, a turning point and a result - so people understand, feel and remember why the venture matters. How to apply Choose one customer as the hero → show a vivid problem moment → present your solution as the guide → prove the result with a number → close with a clear ask. Hero Struggle Guide Plan Success A real customer The problem moment Your venture How the product helps Result and stakes Do Use concrete scenes and plain words. Pair one human example with one number. Keep the customer as hero. Avoid result. Jargon, feature lists, making the founder the hero, and stories with no stakes or no Takeaway: Data convinces the mind; story moves the decision. Use one real customer story and one proof number together. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 21

t: Storytelling - Three Examples UNIT V Dollar Shave Club USA • 2012 • launch video Situation Men paid high prices for razors from a few big brands, and the category felt dull. What they did Founder Michael Dubin starred in a short, humorous launch video made for about $4,500 that mocked overpriced razors and explained the subscription simply. It brought 12,000 orders in 48 hours and crashed the site. Unilever bought the company in 2016 for a reported $1 billion. Paper Boat India • 2013 • nostalgia brand Situation Indian packaged drinks were dominated by colas and juices; drinks like jaljeera and aamras were made only at home. What they did Hector Beverages launched Paper Boat with the tagline "Drinks and Memories". The name, packaging and illustrations evoke childhood - paper boats, summer holidays - and drinks use familiar names. It began on social media with shareable nostalgia. Amul India • since 1966 • ongoing story Situation A farmers' cooperative needed to keep its butter brand familiar to millions of households. What they did Since 1966 the "Amul girl" hoardings have commented on news and everyday events with a witty line, alongside the "Utterly Butterly Delicious" tagline. It is one of the world's longest-running ad campaigns and keeps the brand topical at low cost. Teaching point Tone, a clear "villain" and a simple offer made the story shareable - but operations must keep up. Teaching point A story can create a category: emotion (nostalgia) gives a premium, distinct position. Teaching point A consistent character and voice builds recognition over decades: a story can be a series, not one pitch. Takeaway: A video, a feeling and a character - three ways to tell a startup story. Each worked because it was simple and consistent. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 22

subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Elevator Pitch & Investor Pitch UNIT V Definition An elevator pitch is a 30-60 second summary that earns a follow-up. An investor pitch is a longer, structured presentation (10-15 minutes plus Q&A that asks for a decision. How to apply Formula for 30 seconds: For (customer who [problem], [Company] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [alternative], we [difference]. We have [proof]. We seek [ask]. Investor pitch flow Hook (30 s) → Problem → Solution & demo → Market → Business model → Traction → Competition → Team → Financials & ask. Then 10+ minutes of Q&A. Questions investors ask How will you get customers, and at what cost? What are your margins? What if a big player copies you? What will you do with the money? 1. Write it out Draft the 30-second and 5-minute versions. 2. Time it Rehearse with a timer; trim to fit. 3. Record & review Watch for jargon, filler and speed. 4. Mock Q&A Ask a friendly panel to challenge you. Takeaway: Practice makes a pitch confident: aim to say it clearly in 30 seconds, convincingly in 5 minutes and defensibly under questions. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 23

subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Elevator & Investor Pitch - Three Examples UNIT V Airbnb's one-liner USA • the 30-second core Situation Before anyone reads a deck, founders must explain the business in one sentence. Revamp Moto India • Shark Tank India S1 • negotiation Situation The founders asked R1 crore for 1% equity - an implied valuation of R100 crore. YC Rehearsal Day USA • practice before the pitch Situation Before Demo Day, YC founders practise in front of partners in a dress rehearsal a week earlier. What they did Airbnb's 2009 deck opened with "Book rooms with locals, rather than hotels". In a few words it states the customer action (book), the product (rooms) and the difference (locals, not hotels). Analysts often cite it as a model one-line pitch. What they did After negotiation, Aman Gupta and Anupam Mittal agreed to invest 71 crore for 1.5% - an implied valuation of about 167 crore. The move from 1% to 1.5% shows how valuation is negotiated live during the pitch. What they did Paul Graham's essay "How to Present to Investors" tells founders to focus on two goals: explain what you are doing, and explain why users will want it. Demo Day slots were once ten minutes and later only a few - so the message must be crisp. Teaching point Test your one-liner on a stranger: if they can repeat it back, it works. Teaching point Know your valuation logic and your minimum acceptable terms before you walk in; numbers can move. Teaching point Rehearse with critical listeners and cut everything that does not serve the two core goals. Takeaway: A one-line core, a defended valuation and a rehearsed message - the three habits of pitches that survive questions. Entrepreneurship • Innovation • Startup Ecosystem 24

label: Types of Innovation deck, slide 3

t: Incremental Innovation Definition Small, continuous improvements to an existing product, service, or process - low risk, builds on what already works, often driven by customer feedback. Key Traits • Improves efficiency, quality, or features • Doesn't change the fundamental business model or market • Common in mature industries • Lower risk, lower cost, faster to implement Types of Innovation - Class Session

label: Types of Innovation deck, slide 4
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Incremental Innovation - Examples New iPhone models each year (better camera, faster chip, same core concept) Toothpaste tube with a flip-top cap instead of a screw cap Car manufacturers adding better fuel efficiency each model year Software apps releasing regular feature updates (new emoji, dark mode) Mini-Discussion (think-pair-share) "What's an incremental improvement you've noticed recently in a product you use daily?" Types of Innovation — Class Session

label: Types of Innovation deck, slide 5
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Disruptive Innovation Definition A new product/service that initially targets an overlooked or underserved segment, then improves over time and eventually displaces established competitors. Key Traits Often starts "worse" by traditional metrics, but solves a different problem Creates a new market or value network Can dismantle industry leaders who dismiss it as "not good enough" for mainstream customers Higher risk, potentially transformative reward Types of Innovation - Class Session

subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Disruptive Innovation - Examples Netflix (mail DVDs → streaming) disrupting Blockbuster Ride-sharing apps (Uber/Ola) disrupting traditional taxis Digital cameras disrupting film photography (Kodak) Low-cost airlines disrupting full-service carriers Mini-Discussion (think-pair-share) "Can you think of an industry that got disrupted — and what the 'old guard' failed to see coming?" label: Types of Innovation deck, slide 7
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: - Frugal Innovation Definition Doing more with less - creating simpler, more affordable solutions, often for resource-constrained markets, by rethinking design rather than just cutting features. Key Traits • Focuses on affordability and accessibility • Strips down to core functionality without sacrificing essential value • Often emerges from emerging markets, then moves to developed markets ("reverse innovation") • Resourcefulness over lavish R&D budgets Types of Innovation - Class Session 9

label: Types of Innovation deck, slide 8
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: Frugal Innovation - Examples Tata Nano (low-cost car for the Indian market) Jaipur Foot (low-cost, functional prosthetic limb) M-Pesa mobile money (banking via basic mobile phones in Kenya) Aakash tablet (low-cost tablet for Indian students) Mini-Discussion (think-pair-share) "Why might a frugal innovation from one market succeed in a completely different market later?" t: Compare & Categorize Activity small groups of 3-4 Instructions • Sort each example into Incremental / Disruptive / Frugal Justify their choice in one sentence Flag any example that could fit more than one category - many real innovations blend types Sample items to sort Electric toothbrush with a new bristle pattern A budget smartphone stripped of extra features for a developing market A subscription-based software (SaaS) replacing boxed software Solar lanterns for off-grid villages A new flavor of an existing snack A telemedicine app reaching rural patients with no nearby clinics Types of Innovation — Class Session 11

t: 6. Reflection Activity 10 minutes total Part A - Individual Reflection (5 min, written) Ask participants to write brief responses (a few sentences each) to: Which of the three innovation types feels most relevant to your current work, studies, or an idea you have? Why? Describe a problem you've encountered where a frugal solution (rather than a high-tech one) might work best. Has anything in your field been - or is at risk of being — disruptively replaced? What would you do about it? Types of Innovation - Class Session 12

label: Types of Innovation deck, slide 11
subject: entrepreneur-mindset
t: 6. Reflection Activity (cont.) Part B - Pair Share (5 min) "Share one reflection answer. Then help each other brainstorm: what would an incremental, a disruptive, and a frugal improvement look like for the same problem?" Wrap-Up & Takeaways 5 minutes Key synthesis points to state aloud: • Innovation isn't one-size-fits-all — the right type depends on your goal, resources, and market. • Incremental = improve what exists. Disruptive = change the game. Frugal = do more with less. • Many real breakthroughs combine elements of all three. t: Relation between KR and inference • Knowledge Representation (KR) is a way to store knowledge about the world in a form that a computer system can use to solve complex tasks like diagnosing a disease, having a conversation, or driving a car. • Inference is the process of deriving logical conclusions from given information or known facts. • Together, KR and inference allow systems to reason about information and make decisions based on that information.

E.g., Guitars contains strings, trumpets are brass instruments. • Events: Events are the actions which occur in our world. • Performance: It describe behavior which involves knowledge about how to do things. • Meta-knowledge: It is knowledge about what we know. • Facts: Facts are the truths about the real world and what we represent. • Knowledge-Base: The central component of the knowledge-based agents is the knowledge base. It is represented as KB. The Knowledgebase is a group of the Sentences (Here, sentences are used as a technical term and not identical with the English language).

t: Case Study: Al-Powered Health Diagnostics System • A hospital implements an Al diagnostic system to assist doctors in diagnosing diseases based on patient data, imaging scans, and medical history. The system uses various types of knowledge to provide accurate and reliable diagnostic support.

label: Knowledge Representation notes, p. 12
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Type Knowledge Declarative Knowledge of | Main Emphasis Facts and object details Structural Knowledge Relationships objects between Procedural Knowledge Rules and procedures Heuristic Knowledge Rules of thumb or practical shortcuts Meta Knowledge Knowledge managing knowledge about other Explanation of Example The system uses declarative knowledge to identify symptoms and disease characteristics, such as "High fever and chills could indicate malaria." This factual knowledge helps the AI to recognize patterns in symptoms. Structural knowledge is applied to understand the relationships between symptoms, conditions, and treatments. For example, the Al understands that "a persistent cough is a symptom of respiratory diseases" and can relate symptoms to possible diseases based on medical ontologies. The system follows procedural knowledge to analyze patient data. For example, it runs a specific algorithm to detect anomalies in MRI scans, following a sequence of image- processing steps to highlight suspicious areas for further review. Heuristic knowledge is applied to make quick decisions, such as "If a patient shows symptoms of high blood pressure and is over 60, recommend a cardiovascular check-up." This rule-of-thumb helps prioritize patient screenings and reduces the load on doctors. Meta knowledge is used to evaluate the system's performance, such as monitoring diagnostic accuracy or false-positive rates. Based on these metrics, the system's algorithms are regularly adjusted and improved to ensure better accuracy over time

t: Logical Representation • Logical representation uses formal logic to represent knowledge in a clear, precise. and unambiguous way. • This form is helpful for automated reasoning because it is structured and follows consistent rules. There are different types of logical representations in Al, mainly: • Propositional Logic (Boolean logic): Basic statements that are either true or false. • Predicate Logic (First-order logic): More expressive than propositional logic; allows reasoning about objects and their relationships. Key Components of Logical Representation: • Syntax: The structure and rules of the language (how sentences are formed). • Semantics: The meaning behind the symbols and structures (what the sentences mean). Inference Rules: Rules to derive new knowledge from existing statements (e.g., modus ponens, modus tollens).

PVQ • NOT (-): Inverts the truth value. -P • IMPLIES (→): True unless the first operand is true and the second is false. P → Q • BI-CONDITIONAL (<›): True if both operands are either true or false. t: What is Problem Reduction in Al? • Problem reduction in Artificial Intelligence (Al) refers to breaking down a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems. • These sub-problems are simpler to solve, and their solutions can be combined to form the solution to the original, more complex problem. • This technique helps reduce the overall complexity of the problem and is commonly used in Al to improve the efficiency of problem-solving.

That is called is Problem Reduction. • This method generates arc which is called as AND arcs. One AND arc may point to any number of successor nodes, all of which must be solved for an arc to point to a solution. label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 4
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key problem reduction techniques in Al • Divide and Conquer: - This is a strategy where the problem is divided into smaller, independent sub-problems. After solving each sub-problem, their solutions are combined to solve the original problem. - This method makes complex problems easier to solve by tackling smaller pieces first. - Example: In sorting algorithms like merge sort, the array is divided into smaller arrays, sorted individually, and then merged.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 5
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key problem reduction techniques in Al • Recursive Problem Solving: - In many Al systems, problems are recursively reduced into smaller problems. - For example, in game playing (like chess), Al reduces the problem of determining the best move by recursively considering future moves. - The recursion continues until the problem becomes trivial (i.e., a base case or easily solvable sub-problem).

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 6
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key problem reduction techniques in Al • Search Trees: - Problem reduction is visualized in search trees, where each node represents a sub-problem. The tree explores different paths that lead to solving the overall problem. - AND-OR trees are used in problem reduction, where AND nodes require all sub-problems to be solved, while OR nodes require solving only one sub-problem.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 7
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: And-Or Tree • AND-OR trees are a problem-solving technique used in Artificial Intelligence (Al) to represent the decomposition of complex problems into smaller sub-problems. • These trees are particularly useful for representing problems where some tasks must be completed together (AND) and others can be solved by choosing one of several options (OR). • AND-OR trees are commonly used in search algorithms, decision-making processes, planning, and reasoning.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 8
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Components of AND-OR Trees • Nodes: - Each node in an AND-OR tree represents a state or sub-problem that needs to be solved. - Nodes can be categorized as either: • AND nodes: Represent situations where all child nodes (sub-problems) must be solved to solve the parent node. • OR nodes: Represent situations where solving one of the child nodes is sufficient to solve the parent node.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 9
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Components of AND-OR Trees • Branches (Edges): - Branches connect nodes and represent actions or transitions between different states. - The edges leading from an AND node represent the individual tasks or steps required to complete the AND sub-problems, while edges from an OR node represent alternative solutions or paths.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 10
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Key Components of AND-OR Trees • Leaf Nodes: - Leaf nodes represent terminal states, which can either be goal states (solutions) or failure states. - If the leaf node is a solution state, it means the problem has been solved. If it is a failure state, that path does not lead to a solution.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 11
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Structure of AND-OR Trees • AND Nodes: - The parent node is solved only when all its child nodes (sub-problems) are solved. - Example: If a problem is broken into three sub-tasks, you must solve each of the three tasks (child nodes) to solve the parent problem. - Visually, the solution path from an AND node includes all branches that stem from it.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 12
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Structure of AND-OR Trees • OR Nodes: - The parent node is solved when any one of its child nodes (sub-problems) is solved. - Example: If a decision can be made based on one of three alternative solutions, solving any of the three sub-problems is sufficient to solve the parent problem. - Visually, the solution path from an OR node includes one of the branches stemming from it.

label: Problem Reduction deck, slide 13
subject: foundation-of-ai
t: Example of an AND-OR Tree • Let's take the example of a robot that needs to reach a goal (e.g., picking up an object) but has multiple strategies to choose from. • Problem: - The robot can either take Path A or Path B to reach the object (OR choice). - If the robot chooses Path A, it needs to do two things: avoid obstacles and activate the arm (AND condition). - If the robot chooses Path B, it needs to check the power and then go to the goal (AND condition).
